items.title: Buddy Tate interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995
items.q: And maybe four or five trombones. There’s Sweets and Buck. Vic Dickenson, Dan Minor.

ctx.x: What size was the band at that time? Who was —

Well, we got about one, two, three, got five saxes. One, two three. Let’s see Prez, Jack, yeah, there’s five saxes. One, two, three, four, five. Five saxophones. And maybe four or five trombones. There’s Sweets and Buck. Vic Dickenson, Dan Minor.
It seems to me that the players at that time were not only good players, but real personalities.

items.title: 67395_Vic Dickenson oral history interview
items.q: they featured Prez and Buddy and Jo and Buck and Dickie and...

ctx.x: Were you doing a lot of stage shows then?

Yeah. And that beam would get right into my eye. And I'd have to close them, because I couldn't hardly see the music on account of this bright light in my eye. And so, then I didn't have no solo to play, so...you know, there I was. Usually in them stage shows that we had to play, they featured Prez and Buddy and Jo and Buck and Dickie and...
Was he a lot different after the experience in the Army?

Yeah, yeah. He was. They kind of changed him a bit. You know, actually, to me, his best recording, the two best recordings after the Army were the one he made, that 'D.B. Blues' he and Vic, and he and Buddy Rich and Nat King Cole.
